lessons.title: Probiotics, prebiotics and co.: definitions, strain and label
lessons.objective: Use the consensus definitions of probiotic, prebiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic, explain why evidence is strain-specific, and read a product's label, dose and safety according to WGO.
lessons.closing: Probiotic alive, postbiotic inanimate, prebiotic a substrate; all with a demonstrated benefit. Evidence is tied to the strain and its dose. Label with strain and count at the use-by date; there is no general dose. Immunocompromised: only strains with proven safety.

lessons.title: Vaginal microbiota and bacterial vaginosis
lessons.objective: Diagnose BV with Amsel, Nugent or Hay–Ison, know when not to test, treat and prevent recurrence under CDC and IUSTI, answer questions about partners and probiotics, and explain what Lactobacillus dominance does and does not mean for fertility.
lessons.closing: Amsel 3 of 4; Gram stain is the reference. Without symptoms, no routine testing (IUSTI treats BV found in some high-risk pregnant women and before invasive procedures). Metronidazole or clindamycin; recurrence: suppressive vaginal metronidazole. Male partner: do not treat. Probiotics: not supported by CDC, insufficient evidence for IUSTI. Vaginal microbiota in infertility: research only (ESHRE).

lessons.title: Endometrial microbiome, chronic endometritis and commercial tests
lessons.objective: Explain why ESHRE and NICE do not recommend endometrial microbiome profiling, where they disagree on chronic endometritis in implantation failure, and what the 2025 consensus says about commercial microbiome tests.
lessons.closing: Uterine and vaginal microbiome in RIF: not recommended (ESHRE). NICE: do not offer endometrial microbiome analysis as an add-on for any embryo transfer (silent on the vaginal microbiome). Chronic endometritis: can be considered with antibiotics in RIF (ESHRE); do not offer its analysis as a transfer add-on (NICE); no standard threshold. Stool tests: insufficient evidence for routine use and no advice from the provider.

items.title: Probiotic, prebiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic: the consensus definitions
items.core: According to the ISAPP definitions set out in its 2020 synbiotics consensus, probiotics are “live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host”, and a prebiotic is “a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit”. [[ref:isapp-2020-synbiotics]] A synbiotic is “a mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit on the host”. [[ref:isapp-2020-synbiotics]] A postbiotic is a “preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host”. [[ref:isapp-2021-postbiotics]]
items.body:
A synbiotic can be complementary (a probiotic plus a prebiotic, each meeting its own criteria) or synergistic (the substrate is designed to be used by the co-administered microorganism); either way the combination must show a benefit in an appropriately designed trial. [[ref:isapp-2020-synbiotics]] Postbiotics are deliberately inactivated microbial cells, with or without metabolites or cell components; purified metabolites (for example butyric acid or lactic acid) and vaccines are not postbiotics. [[ref:isapp-2021-postbiotics]]

The 2023 WGO guideline uses the same definitions of probiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic, but its definitions table keeps an older wording for prebiotic: “a selectively fermented ingredient that results in specific changes in the composition and/or activity of the gastrointestinal microbiota, thus conferring benefit(s) upon host health”. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] It also discourages terms such as paraprobiotic, immunobiotic or “ghost probiotic” because they lack clear definitions. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: Which word separates a postbiotic from a probiotic, and why is purified butyric acid not a postbiotic?
items.pearl: All four definitions end the same way: “confers a health benefit”. Without that demonstrated benefit, the label does not apply.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ISAPP consensus definitions (probiotic 2014, prebiotic 2017, synbiotic 2020, postbiotic 2021) taken from the definitions box of the synbiotics consensus and from the postbiotics consensus; the 2014 and 2017 papers were not read directly. WGO 2023, Table 1 (pp. 4–5). These are definitions, not graded recommendations.

items.title: The effect is shown strain by strain
items.core: For WGO 2023, the most robust way to assess a probiotic is to link each benefit to specific strains, or strain combinations, at the effective dose, and clinical recommendations should tie specific strains to the claimed benefit based on human studies. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] That is why the strain designation (for example, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG ATCC 53103) is part of the product's identity. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.body:
WGO describes an emerging concept: some mechanisms, such as colonisation resistance, regulation of transit or normalising a perturbed microbiota, may be shared across strains, species or even genera. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] Pooling different strains in a meta-analysis is valid only if a shared mechanism is shown to explain the benefit; otherwise the evidence should be strain-specific. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]

In 2020 the genus Lactobacillus was restructured and 23 new genera were defined: for example, Lactobacillus rhamnosus became Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, whereas L. crispatus, L. gasseri and L. acidophilus remain in Lactobacillus. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: When does WGO accept applying the result of a mixed-strain meta-analysis to a single strain?
items.pearl: Faced with a bottle, look for the strain (the letters and numbers after the species): without it you cannot look up the evidence.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: WGO 2023, section 1 (pp. 4–8): descriptive guideline text, no recommendation grade.

items.title: Label, dose and safety of a probiotic
items.core: WGO 2023 asks that the label state genus and species (and subspecies) using current nomenclature, the strain designation, the viable count of each strain at the end of shelf-life, storage conditions, a recommended dose based on the effect, a description of the effect and a contact for post-market surveillance. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] There is no general dose: many products deliver 1–10 billion CFU per dose, but Bifidobacterium longum 35624 was effective in IBS at 100 million CFU/day and other products need 300–450 billion CFU three times daily. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.body:
Because most are not made to pharmaceutical standards, regulators may not oversee their quality, and some products fail to meet label claims for the number and type of viable microbes; WGO advises reliable manufacturers that state the dose at the use-by date. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] What the label may claim depends on regional regulation; most are sold as foods or supplements and typically cannot mention disease. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]

On safety, the pathogenic potential of lactobacilli is considered quite low and bifidobacteria have a similar record, but in people with compromised immunity or serious underlying disease use should be restricted to strains and indications with proven safety and efficacy in that population. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: Which seven items should a probiotic label carry according to WGO?
items.pearl: The number that matters is the one at the use-by date, not at manufacture.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: WGO 2023, sections 2.1–2.3 (pp. 11–13): descriptive good practice, no grade. The doses quoted are the guideline's examples, not recommended regimens for gynaecological indications.

items.title: Bacterial vaginosis: a dysbiosis, often without symptoms
items.core: CDC 2021 defines bacterial vaginosis as a vaginal dysbiosis in which hydrogen peroxide- and lactic acid-producing Lactobacillus species are replaced by high concentrations of anaerobes (G. vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, A. vaginae and others), with a polymicrobial biofilm on the epithelium. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] It is the most common cause of vaginal discharge worldwide, yet in a nationally representative survey most women with BV were asymptomatic. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.body:
IUSTI 2018 adds that it can arise and remit spontaneously and is not strictly considered a sexually transmitted infection, although it is associated with sexual activity; the G. vaginalis biofilm seems key in the switch from normal flora to BV. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] CDC links it to new or multiple partners, female partners, lack of condom use, douching and copper IUDs; hormonal contraception does not increase the risk and might protect, and vitamin D deficiency has not been reported as a risk factor. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]

It is associated with higher risk of acquiring STIs (HIV, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, trichomonas, M. genitalium, HPV and HSV-2), complications after gynaecological surgery and complications of pregnancy; CDC states that all women with BV should be tested for HIV and other STIs. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: What replaces Lactobacillus in BV, and what share of women with BV have no symptoms according to CDC?
items.pearl: No symptoms does not rule out BV, but, as you will see, it does not oblige you to look for it either.

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Bacterial Vaginosis” section (narrative text; HIV/STI testing is stated as a management instruction, ungraded). IUSTI 2018, p. 2.

items.title: Diagnosing BV: Amsel, Nugent and Hay–Ison
items.core: Amsel requires at least 3 of 4 criteria: homogeneous thin discharge, clue cells on microscopy, vaginal pH > 4.5 and a fishy odour before or after adding 10% KOH. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] Gram stain is the reference method: a Nugent score of 0–3 is consistent with Lactobacillus-predominant microbiota, 4–6 with intermediate microbiota and 7–10 with BV. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
Against Nugent, CDC gives Amsel a sensitivity of 37–70% and specificity of 94–99%; IUSTI quotes a sensitivity of 60–72% against Gram stain. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] IUSTI recommends microscopy with the Hay–Ison criteria, quicker in practice, as the current best test (strength 1, quality A): grade 1 normal (lactobacilli predominate), 2 intermediate and 3 BV; grades 0 (suggests recent antibiotics) and 4 (aerobic vaginitis flora) are not related to BV. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]

IUSTI notes that Nugent does not take into account morphotypes not associated with BV and that “intermediate flora” has unclear clinical implications, although it is associated with complications. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.recall: What are the four Amsel criteria, and which Nugent scores define normal, intermediate and BV?
items.pearl: A pH > 4.5 suggests BV or trichomoniasis and is almost always normal in candidiasis (IUSTI).

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Diagnostic Considerations” (no formal grading). IUSTI 2018, pp. 3–4: Hay–Ison, strength grade 1, quality grade A (the guideline uses strength 1–2 and quality A–C; the extracted text does not include the legend for these grades).

items.title: Molecular BV panels: only with symptoms
items.core: CDC 2021 states that BV nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), which detect G. vaginalis, A. vaginae, BVAB2, Megasphaera type 1 and certain lactobacilli, should be used only in symptomatic women, because their accuracy is not well defined in asymptomatic women. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 states that asymptomatic women do not require testing for BV, aerobic vaginitis or candida. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
Of the five quantitative multiplex assays CDC lists, two are FDA cleared and three are laboratory-developed tests that must be validated internally; traditional methods (Amsel, Nugent) remain useful because of lower cost and rapid results. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] Culture of G. vaginalis is not recommended because it is not specific, and cervical cytology has no utility for diagnosing BV. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]

The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing adds that multiplex PCR and cultures, although potentially useful, are not microbiome testing and cannot be used as a proxy for microbiome profiling (90% agreement), and that samples other than faeces, including vaginal swabs, should be processed according to existing scientific evidence and clinical indications (97.5%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: In which women does CDC accept a BV NAAT, and what does IUSTI say about asymptomatic women?
items.pearl: A “wellness” vaginal panel in a woman without symptoms has no indication in any of these sources.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Diagnostic Considerations” (ungraded). IUSTI 2018, p. 3 (text). Porcari 2025, Table 1, statements 13 and 11 (Delphi, expert opinion; consensus threshold ≥ 80%).

items.title: Treating BV: CDC versus IUSTI
items.core: CDC 2021 recommends treating symptomatic women with metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole gel 0.75% (5 g) intravaginally once daily for 5 days or clindamycin cream 2% (5 g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 recommends as first line 5–7 days of oral (400–500 mg twice daily) or topical metronidazole, or 7 days of intravaginal clindamycin, depending on preference and circumstances (strength 1, quality A). [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
As alternatives, CDC lists oral clindamycin or ovules, secnidazole 2 g single dose and tinidazole; IUSTI lists metronidazole 2 g single dose, tinidazole, oral clindamycin and dequalinium chloride 10 mg vaginal tablet for 6 days. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] IUSTI notes that single-dose regimens cure less often than longer ones. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]

Indications differ: CDC treats symptomatic women; IUSTI adds some pregnant women with positive microscopy and a history of idiopathic preterm birth or second-trimester loss, and women undergoing gynaecological surgery or invasive diagnostic procedures, and leaves treating asymptomatic women with positive microscopy as optional. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] CDC considers avoiding alcohol with metronidazole unnecessary and warns that clindamycin cream may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms for 5 days. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: Which three regimens does CDC recommend, and in which asymptomatic situations does IUSTI treat?
items.pearl: Seven days of oral metronidazole is the regimen common to both guidelines; single dose cures less often.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Treatment” (recommended and alternative regimens, no formal grade). IUSTI 2018, pp. 5–6: first line strength 1, quality A. The IUSTI website lists this guideline as “Under review” (accessed 14-10-2026): an update may exist that was not read.

items.title: Recurrent BV: suppression with metronidazole
items.core: After 7 days of oral metronidazole, a longitudinal study cited by IUSTI found recurrence rates of 23% at one month, 43% at 3 months and 58% at 12 months. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] IUSTI recommends intravaginal metronidazole as the current best treatment for persistent and recurrent BV (strength 2, quality B). [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
CDC accepts repeating the same regimen or switching; with multiple recurrences, metronidazole gel 0.75% or a 750 mg metronidazole vaginal suppository twice weekly for > 3 months reduces recurrences, although the benefit does not persist once stopped. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] With limited data, it mentions an oral nitroimidazole for 7 days followed by intravaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days and metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4–6 months, and monthly oral metronidazole 2 g with fluconazole 150 mg. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]

IUSTI also cites a small trial of intravaginal lactate gel (5 ml for 3 days after menses, for 6 months): 88% free of BV versus 10% with placebo. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] CDC does not recommend high-dose vitamin D to prevent recurrence and warns that douching might increase relapse. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: Which treatment does IUSTI prefer for recurrent BV, and what happens when suppression stops according to CDC?
items.pearl: Suppression works while it lasts: warn that the benefit does not persist once it is stopped.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: IUSTI 2018, pp. 6–7: strength 2, quality B. CDC 2021, “Follow-Up” (ungraded text; several options with limited data).

items.title: Treat the partner? Not routinely
items.core: CDC 2021 does not recommend routine treatment of sex partners, because it does not change the woman's response or recurrence; a phase 3 trial of 7 days of oral metronidazole for male partners of women with recurrent BV did not reduce recurrence. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 recommends that male partners do not require treatment and that female partners may be treated if they have BV (strength 2, quality B). [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body: In women who have sex with women, partners' microbiota are often concordant: IUSTI considers it reasonable to check and treat the regular partner if she has BV, although there is no evidence that this reduces recurrence, and CDC notes that no studies have evaluated treating female partners. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] CDC cites a pilot study in which treating the male partner (oral metronidazole plus topical clindamycin on the penis) changed the vaginal microbiota, and notes that in the phase 3 trial women whose partners adhered had fewer treatment failures; even so, it maintains that routine treatment is not recommended. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: What do CDC and IUSTI say about treating male and female partners?
items.pearl: In a couple trying to conceive, treating the man “just in case” has no support from either guideline.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Management of Sex Partners” (ungraded). IUSTI 2018, pp. 9–10: strength 2, quality B.

items.title: Probiotics for BV: the evidence falls short
items.core: CDC 2021 concludes that no studies support probiotics (intravaginal Lactobacillus or other formulations) as an adjunctive or replacement therapy for BV. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 cites a systematic review that found insufficient evidence for or against them, and a later meta-analysis that found them effective for treating and preventing BV but with studies of variable quality; it calls for more good-quality research. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
The most promising data are still investigational: vaginal L. crispatus CTV-05 (Lactin-V), daily for 4 days in week 1 then twice weekly for 10 weeks after 5 days of metronidazole gel, substantially lowered recurrence at 12 weeks versus placebo, but according to CDC it was not FDA cleared or commercially available. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] WGO 2023, a gastroenterology guideline, mentions outside its scope that numerous studies show probiotics can reduce BV, without recommending a strain or regimen. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]

In short: CDC does not support probiotics for BV; IUSTI considers the evidence insufficient or of variable quality; WGO mentions them without a recommendation. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: What do CDC, IUSTI and WGO say about probiotics in BV?
items.pearl: A probiotic does not replace the recommended antibiotic: according to CDC, no studies support it as a replacement or an adjunct.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Treatment” and “Follow-Up” (text, ungraded). IUSTI 2018, p. 7 (text; no graded recommendation on probiotics). WGO 2023, p. 16 (mention outside its scope, ungraded). None of these sources assesses probiotics for fertility outcomes.

items.title: Lactobacillus dominance and fertility: what it means and what it does not
items.core: A Nugent score of 0–3 is consistent with Lactobacillus-predominant microbiota. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] The ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility guideline considers that vaginal microbiota testing in these couples could be considered only in a research setting (rec. 15, “research only”): evidence for a role of abnormal microbiota is insufficient and there is no evidence that correcting it improves fertility outcomes. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
The studies it reviews are case–control and cohort studies, using different detection methods (microscopy, Spiegel criteria, Nugent, qPCR), sampling at different points of the cycle or treatment, and a definition of “Lactobacillus dominance” that varies between papers. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document notes that Lactobacillus is part of the physiological flora, but that it is unclear whether an unfavourable microbiome disrupts implantation itself or is a marker of another factor. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline describes an association between vaginal dysbiosis (greater diversity and lack of lactobacilli) and recurrent loss, but there are no studies on its predictive value. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about vaginal microbiota testing in unexplained infertility, and why?
items.pearl: A “low Lactobacillus” result in a woman without symptoms is not an infertility diagnosis, and ESHRE notes there is no evidence that correcting the vaginal microbiota improves fertility.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility, rec. 15 (p. 48), “Research only”; justification p. 49. ESHRE RIF 2023, “Microbiome profiling” (good practice, no GRADE). ESHRE 2022 RPL, section 1.4 (text, no recommendation).

items.title: Endometrial and vaginal microbiome profiling: not routinely
items.core: The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document does not recommend uterine or vaginal microbiome profiling. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] NICE NG257 (2026) advises not offering endometrial receptivity testing as a treatment add-on for embryo transfer, including microbiological analysis (for example, endometrial microbiome metagenomic analysis). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE acknowledges associations (a meta-analysis of six cohort studies with 1,095 women, among other studies, linked dysbiotic microbiota to poorer reproductive outcomes), but lists what is missing: the optimal method of assessment, the stability and spontaneous resolution of an unfavourable microbiome, its changes during the cycle and IVF, the efficacy of interventions, and whether it is a cause or a marker. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] In a study of 145 women with RIF and 21 controls, lactobacilli were lower in the vagina but not in the endometrium. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

NICE found no evidence on treating endometrial abnormalities related to the microbiome and made a research recommendation: whether treatments based on these analyses, such as antibiotics for endometritis or microbiota transplantation, improve assisted reproduction outcomes. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What do ESHRE (RIF) and NICE NG257 say about endometrial microbiome analysis?
items.pearl: In the survey ESHRE cites, 47% of clinicians considered dysbiosis relevant in implantation failure: practice is running ahead of the evidence.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE RIF 2023, “Microbiome profiling”: red level, “not recommended” (not routinely offered; per ESHRE this does not mean forbidden in all circumstances). NICE NG257, 1.41.1 [2026] (pp. 46–47) and research recommendation 1 (p. 60).

items.title: Chronic endometritis: ESHRE allows it to be considered; NICE does not offer it as an add-on
items.core: The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document states that assessment for chronic endometritis can be considered and, if diagnosed, antibiotic treatment can be considered. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] NICE NG257 advises not offering microbiological analysis, including analysis of infectious chronic endometritis, as an add-on for embryo transfer. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline concludes that prospective studies and randomised trials are needed before screening for endometritis can be recommended. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
It is diagnosed by hysteroscopy, haematoxylin and eosin staining and CD138 immunohistochemistry, as well as chromohysteroscopy, culture and molecular techniques, but there is no standardised plasma cell threshold (for example, > 1 or > 5 per high-power field) and studies are often small or lack controls. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] Reviews of antibiotics conflict: one found higher live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates with cured versus persistent endometritis (OR 5.33; 95% CI 2.41–11.79), another found no significant difference (OR 2.90; 95% CI 0.65–12.98) and a third concluded that oral antibiotics did not improve pregnancy or live birth. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

In recurrent pregnancy loss, reported prevalence ranges from 7% to 58% depending on the method, the only study with fertile controls found no difference, and the effect of antibiotics has not been tested in randomised trials. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Where do ESHRE (RIF) and NICE disagree on chronic endometritis, and why is the antibiotic evidence conflicting?
items.pearl: If you test for it in implantation failure, agree with the patient beforehand on what you will do with the result: neither the threshold nor the antibiotic regimen is standardised in these sources.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: ESHRE RIF 2023, “Investigating chronic endometritis”: orange level, “can be considered” (good practice, no GRADE). NICE NG257, 1.41.1 [2026]: “do not offer”; it applies to any embryo transfer (NG257 does not specifically address recurrent implantation failure). ESHRE 2022 RPL, section 1.4: conclusion without a graded recommendation. None specifies an antibiotic regimen.

items.title: Commercial gut microbiome tests: what the 2025 consensus says
items.core: The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing (69 experts, Delphi method) concludes that there is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine use of these tests in clinical practice (90% agreement) and discourages patients from requesting them directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice in the report (98%) and states that any change in management should be made only by the referring professional (100%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.body:
On report content, it discourages the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), considers that there is insufficient evidence to include any dysbiosis index (90%) and that generally there is not enough information to report strict healthy reference ranges of species abundance (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It also does not recommend metabolomic analysis of biofluids in clinical practice and discourages inferring the microbiome's “metabolic potential” from the taxonomic profile (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]

The panel warns that direct-to-consumer tests have proliferated without regulatory consensus or proven clinical value, with potential waste of resources and drawbacks in the clinical management of patients. [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: Which three elements of a commercial microbiome report does the 2025 consensus discourage?
items.pearl: If the report comes with a list of supplements or a diet, that section goes against the consensus itself.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: Porcari 2025, Table 1: statements 32, 6, 30, 3, 26, 27, 28 and 20, with their agreement rates. Expert statements (Delphi, consensus threshold ≥ 80%), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome.

items.stem: According to the 2021 ISAPP consensus, which of these products could be a postbiotic?

options.text: Capsules of purified butyric acid
options.why: Purified metabolites are not postbiotics; they are named by their chemical name.

options.text: A preparation of heat-inactivated lactobacilli with a demonstrated health benefit
options.why: Correct: a preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit.

options.text: Capsules of live bacteria with a demonstrated benefit
options.why: If the microorganisms are alive, it is a probiotic.

options.text: Inulin selectively utilised by the microbiota with a demonstrated benefit
options.why: A selectively utilised substrate with a benefit is a prebiotic.

items.explanation: The key word is “inanimate”: a postbiotic keeps the cell (whole or as components), unlike a purified metabolite.

items.stem: A meta-analysis pools 12 different lactobacillus strains and finds a benefit. According to WGO 2023, when is it valid to apply that result to a specific strain?

options.text: Whenever the strain belongs to the same genus
options.why: Genus is not enough; WGO asks for a shared mechanism to be demonstrated.

options.text: Only if a shared mechanism is shown to explain the benefit; otherwise strain-specific evidence is needed
options.why: Correct: this is the condition WGO sets for mixed-strain meta-analyses.

options.text: If the strain is taken at more than 10 billion CFU
options.why: WGO says no general dose can be stated.

options.text: Never: WGO rejects meta-analyses with several strains
options.why: It does not reject them: they are valid if a shared mechanism is demonstrated.

items.explanation: WGO prefers linking each benefit to specific strains at the effective dose; pooling strains is valid only with a demonstrated shared mechanism.

items.stem: A woman has thin homogeneous discharge, vaginal pH 5.0 and a fishy odour on adding KOH; no microscope is available. Which statement is correct?

options.text: She meets 3 of the 4 Amsel criteria: BV can be diagnosed without microscopy
options.why: Correct: three criteria are clinical, so IUSTI accepts the diagnosis without a microscope.

options.text: Without clue cells it cannot be diagnosed
options.why: Amsel requires 3 of 4, not all 4.

options.text: A PCR panel is needed to confirm
options.why: CDC notes that traditional methods remain useful; PCR is not required.

options.text: A pH > 4.5 points to candidiasis
options.why: IUSTI states that pH > 4.5 suggests BV or trichomoniasis and is almost always normal in candidiasis.

items.explanation: Amsel: homogeneous discharge, pH > 4.5, amine odour and clue cells; 3 are enough.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman (fictional case), with no discharge, odour or itch, undergoing a fertility work-up, asks for a BV PCR panel. What best fits CDC and IUSTI?

options.text: Order it: NAATs are the reference method
options.why: The reference method is Gram stain.

options.text: It is not indicated: CDC reserves NAATs for symptomatic women and IUSTI does not indicate testing asymptomatic women
options.why: Correct: NAAT accuracy is not well defined in asymptomatic women.

options.text: Order a G. vaginalis culture
options.why: CDC does not recommend it because it is not specific.

options.text: Use cervical cytology to rule it out
options.why: According to CDC it has no clinical utility for diagnosing BV.

items.explanation: Without symptoms these guidelines do not indicate looking for BV; IUSTI only contemplates treating asymptomatic BV in some high-risk pregnant women and before invasive procedures (and as an option with positive microscopy).

items.stem: A woman with recurrent BV and a male partner asks whether her partner should be treated. What do CDC and IUSTI indicate?

options.text: Routine 7-day oral metronidazole for the man
options.why: A phase 3 trial showed no reduction in recurrence.

options.text: Do not routinely treat the male partner
options.why: Correct: CDC does not recommend it and IUSTI states he does not require treatment (strength 2, quality B).

options.text: Topical penile clindamycin plus oral metronidazole
options.why: It was only tested in a pilot study; it is not a recommendation.

options.text: Treat only if he has urinary symptoms
options.why: Neither guideline proposes that criterion.

items.explanation: Treating the male partner does not change response or recurrence; with a female partner, IUSTI accepts treating her if she has BV.

items.stem: After a BV episode treated with metronidazole, a patient wants to use a commercial vaginal probiotic instead of the antibiotic next time. Which statement fits the sources?

options.text: CDC lists it as an alternative regimen
options.why: CDC alternatives are antibiotics (clindamycin, secnidazole, tinidazole).

options.text: CDC says no studies support them as adjunct or replacement, and IUSTI considers the evidence insufficient or of variable quality
options.why: Correct: this is how both guidelines summarise it.

options.text: Lactin-V is the standard and commercially available
options.why: According to CDC it was not FDA cleared or commercially available.

options.text: IUSTI recommends them with strength 1 and quality A
options.why: IUSTI makes no graded recommendation in favour of probiotics.

items.explanation: No BV guideline supports replacing the antibiotic with a probiotic.

items.stem: Third episode of BV in a year despite recommended regimens. What does IUSTI 2018 consider the current best treatment for persistent and recurrent BV?

options.text: Intravaginal metronidazole
options.why: Correct: strength 2, quality B.

options.text: High-dose vitamin D
options.why: According to CDC, randomised trials have not shown it to reduce recurrence, and it is not recommended.

options.text: Regular vaginal douching
options.why: According to CDC they may increase relapse.

options.text: Treating the male partner
options.why: It does not reduce recurrence and is not routinely recommended.

items.explanation: CDC describes suppression with metronidazole gel twice weekly for > 3 months, with a benefit that does not persist after stopping.

items.stem: A couple with unexplained infertility asks for vaginal microbiota testing “to see whether lactobacilli are missing”. What does ESHRE 2023 say?

options.text: It is recommended for all couples
options.why: It is not part of the recommended work-up.

options.text: It could be considered only in a research setting
options.why: Correct: rec. 15, “research only”.

options.text: It is recommended if Nugent is intermediate
options.why: The guideline does not propose that indication.

options.text: It is recommended, and if lactobacilli are low, treat with probiotics
options.why: ESHRE states there is no evidence that correcting the microbiota improves fertility.

items.explanation: Heterogeneous methods, different sampling times and no evidence of benefit from correction: hence research only.

items.stem: A woman with recurrent implantation failure and a normal hysteroscopy. Regarding chronic endometritis and the endometrial microbiome, which statement is correct?

options.text: ESHRE recommends CD138 biopsy and microbiome profiling for everyone (green level)
options.why: Endometritis is “can be considered” (orange) and the microbiome “not recommended” (red).

options.text: ESHRE allows assessment for endometritis and antibiotics if diagnosed to be considered; NICE advises not offering that analysis as a transfer add-on
options.why: Correct: this is the disagreement between the two guidelines.

options.text: Both recommend endometrial microbiome profiling before the next transfer
options.why: Both advise against it: ESHRE “not recommended”, NICE “do not offer”.

options.text: There is a standardised threshold of > 5 plasma cells per field
options.why: ESHRE stresses that there is no standardised threshold (> 1 or > 5 depending on the study).

items.explanation: ESHRE (RIF): endometritis “can be considered”, microbiome “not recommended”. NICE NG257: offer neither endometrial microbiome analysis nor infectious chronic endometritis analysis as an add-on.

items.stem: A patient brings a direct-to-consumer stool test reporting an “abnormal Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio” and a supplement plan. According to the 2025 international consensus, what is correct?

options.text: The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio is a validated dysbiosis marker
options.why: The consensus discourages reporting it (86%).

options.text: There is insufficient evidence for routine use, and the consensus discourages both that ratio and therapeutic advice from the provider
options.why: Correct: statements 32, 26 and 30.

options.text: It should be repeated monthly to follow the response to supplements
options.why: The consensus only says longitudinal assessment may be useful in specific clinical scenarios.

options.text: Before repeating it she should stop her medication and change her diet
options.why: The consensus says not to stop therapy or change diet unless the referring physician recommends it.

items.explanation: Any change in management is decided by the referring professional, not the provider.

items.title: Case: Beatriz, Federico and two microbiome tests bought online

steps.text: Beatriz (fictional case), 38, and Federico have had three transfers without implantation; their team considers that they meet ESHRE's definition of recurrent implantation failure, which uses an individual threshold of 60% cumulative predicted chance of implantation. Beatriz brings a vaginal test bought online (“low Lactobacillus”) and a direct-to-consumer stool analysis with a supplement plan. She has no discharge, odour or itch. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

Without symptoms, IUSTI does not indicate BV testing and CDC reserves molecular tests for symptomatic women; ESHRE does not recommend vaginal or uterine microbiome profiling in implantation failure. If microscopy showed BV, IUSTI leaves treating an asymptomatic woman as optional. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

Beatriz asks about chronic endometritis. ESHRE allows assessment and antibiotics if diagnosed to be considered, acknowledging the lack of standardisation; NICE NG257 advises not offering microbiological analysis, including infectious chronic endometritis, as a transfer add-on. You explain both positions and they decide together. If hysteroscopy with biopsy is done and BV is found, IUSTI lists women undergoing invasive diagnostic procedures among the indications for treatment. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]

Regarding the stool test, the 2025 international consensus considers the evidence insufficient for routine use and discourages therapeutic advice from the provider. If she still wants a probiotic, WGO asks for evidence for the specific strain; ESHRE (RIF) lists the efficacy of interventions to improve the microbiome among the unresolved questions, and the ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline notes there is no evidence that correcting the vaginal microbiota improves fertility. [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.authors: Workowski KA, Bachmann LH, Chan PA, Johnston CM, Muzny CA, Park I, Reno H, Zenilman JM, Bolan GA
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.population: People with sexually transmitted infections or related syndromes in the USA; the bacterial vaginosis section is used here. MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(4):1-187.
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.finding: BV: dysbiosis with replacement of Lactobacillus by anaerobes; mostly asymptomatic. Diagnosis by Amsel (3 of 4) or Nugent (Gram stain reference); NAATs only in symptomatic women; no G. vaginalis culture or cytology. Treat symptomatic women: oral metronidazole 7 days, metronidazole gel 5 days or clindamycin cream 7 days. Recurrence: metronidazole gel twice weekly > 3 months. Routine partner treatment not recommended. No studies support probiotics as adjunct or replacement; Lactin-V lowered recurrence in one trial but was not commercially available. High-dose vitamin D not recommended.
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.limitations: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC8344968) read; only the BV section was used. No formal recommendation grading in the text (recommended and alternative regimens). US context; brand names and FDA clearances as of 2021.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment.
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based.

eshre-2023-rif.title: ESHRE good practice recommendations on recurrent implantation failure
eshre-2023-rif.authors: ESHRE Working Group on Recurrent Implantation Failure; Cimadomo D, de los Santos MJ, Griesinger G, Lainas G, Le Clef N, McLernon DJ, Montjean D, Toth B, Vermeulen N, Macklon N
eshre-2023-rif.population: Patients and couples undergoing IVF/ICSI with recurrent implantation failure; Hum Reprod Open 2023 (ESHRE Pages). Assumes a standard fertility work-up completed before ART.
eshre-2023-rif.finding: Defines RIF individually with a 60% threshold of cumulative predicted chance of implantation. 19 recommendations on investigations and 13 on interventions, classed as recommended, to be considered or not recommended. Recommended: review lifestyle, re-assess endometrial thickness, genetic counselling if a chromosomal abnormality is found, antiphospholipid antibodies with risk factors. To be considered: karyotyping, hysteroscopy, chronic endometritis, thyroid, PGT-A, blastocyst transfer. Not recommended: NK cells, cytokines, HLA-C, microbiome, sperm DNA fragmentation, scratching, G-CSF, intralipid, IVIG, PBMC, PRP, intrauterine hCG, heparin, GnRHa/AI pre-treatment, assisted hatching.
eshre-2023-rif.limitations: Full text read in the Europe PMC open-access XML version (PMC10270320); the PDF could not be downloaded and the colour-coded summary figures (images) were not read, only the table wording. Good practice document based on expert opinion supported by the literature and a survey, without GRADE ratings; RIF definitions vary across studies.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

isapp-2020-synbiotics.title: The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) consensus statement on the definition and scope of synbiotics
isapp-2020-synbiotics.authors: Swanson KS, Gibson GR, Hutkins R, Reimer RA, Reid G, Verbeke K, Scott KP, Holscher HD, Azad MB, Delzenne NM, Sanders ME
isapp-2020-synbiotics.population: ISAPP expert panel (nutrition, physiology, microbiology) on the definition and scope of synbiotics; Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2020;17(11):687-701.
isapp-2020-synbiotics.finding: Synbiotic: “a mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit on the host”; complementary (probiotic plus prebiotic) or synergistic (substrate for the co-administered microorganism). Its definitions box also gives the ISAPP definitions of probiotic and prebiotic (“a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit”).
isapp-2020-synbiotics.limitations: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC7581511) read. Expert consensus on terminology and criteria, not a clinical guideline; it does not assess gynaecological indications. The original probiotic (2014) and prebiotic (2017) consensus papers were not read directly.

isapp-2021-postbiotics.title: The International Scientific Association of Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) consensus statement on the definition and scope of postbiotics
isapp-2021-postbiotics.authors: Salminen S, Collado MC, Endo A, Hill C, Lebeer S, Quigley EMM, Sanders ME, Shamir R, Swann JR, Szajewska H, Vinderola G
isapp-2021-postbiotics.population: ISAPP expert panel on the definition and scope of postbiotics; Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021;18(9):649-667.
isapp-2021-postbiotics.finding: Postbiotic: a “preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host”. They are deliberately inactivated microbial cells, with or without metabolites or components; purified metabolites and vaccines are not postbiotics.
isapp-2021-postbiotics.limitations: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC8387231) read. Expert consensus on terminology; it does not assess gynaecological indications. Later publisher and author corrections were not reviewed.

iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.title: 2018 European (IUSTI/WHO) International Union against sexually transmitted infections (IUSTI) World Health Organisation (WHO) guideline on the management of vaginal discharge
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.authors: Sherrard J, Wilson J, Donders G, Mendling W, Jensen JS
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.population: Women with vaginal discharge (bacterial vaginosis, aerobic vaginitis, candidiasis and trichomoniasis) in Europe; Int J STD AIDS 2018;29(13):1258-1272.
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.finding: Asymptomatic women do not need BV testing. Best test: microscopy with Hay–Ison criteria (1A). First line: oral or topical metronidazole 5–7 days or intravaginal clindamycin 7 days (1A). Persistent and recurrent BV: intravaginal metronidazole (2B). Male partners: no treatment; female partners may be treated if they have BV (2B). Pregnancy: clindamycin (2C). Probiotics: a systematic review found insufficient evidence and a later meta-analysis was favourable with studies of variable quality.
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.limitations: Full PDF from the IUSTI website read (15 pp.). Strength “grade 1/2” and quality “grade A–C” with no legend in the extracted text. The IUSTI website lists it as “Under review” (accessed 14-10-2026); an update may exist that was not read.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.title: International consensus statement on microbiome testing in clinical practice
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.authors: Porcari S, Mullish BH, Asnicar F, Ng SC, Zhao L, Hansen R, O'Toole PW, Raes J, Hold G, Putignani L, et al.; Cammarota G, Gasbarrini A, Ianiro G
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.population: Microbiome testing (mainly gut) in clinical practice; 69 experts from 18 countries, Delphi consensus. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025;10(2):154-167.
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.finding: There is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine microbiome testing (90%). It discourages direct patient requests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%), therapeutic advice from the provider (98%), the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), dysbiosis indices (90%) and strict healthy reference ranges (90%). Multiplex PCR and cultures are not microbiome testing (90%); vaginal samples should be processed according to existing evidence and indications (97.5%).
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.limitations: The accepted author manuscript on PMC (PMC12343204) was read, not the typeset version; appendices not included. Expert-opinion statements (Delphi, ≥ 80% threshold), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome rather than vaginal or endometrial microbiome.

wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.title: World Gastroenterology Organisation Global Guidelines: Probiotics and prebiotics
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.authors: Guarner F, Sanders ME, Szajewska H, Cohen H, Eliakim R, Herrera C, Karakan T, Merenstein D, Piscoya A, Ramakrishna B, Salminen S
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.population: Use of probiotics and prebiotics in gastrointestinal health and disease in adults and children; WGO global guideline (February 2023).
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.finding: Definitions of probiotic, prebiotic (older wording), synbiotic and postbiotic. The strongest evidence links each benefit to specific strains at the effective dose; pooling strains is valid only with a demonstrated shared mechanism. The label should state strain, viable count at end of shelf-life and an effect-based dose; there is no general dose. Some products fail label claims; safety is good in healthy people and use is restricted in the immunocompromised. Mentions, outside its scope, that probiotics can reduce bacterial vaginosis.
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.limitations: Full PDF from the WGO website read (52 pp.). Gastroenterology-focused: it does not assess probiotics for gynaecological or fertility indications. Clinical indications use Oxford 2011 levels; general sections are ungraded. A journal version exists (J Clin Gastroenterol 2024;58(6):533-553, DOI 10.1097/MCG.0000000000002002) and was not read.
